interpretation.purpose: A source-level audit trail linking construct boundaries, mathematical feature families, empirical associations, null findings, and validity guardrails.
interpretation.formula_rule: A feature formula is authorized only by a primary application or a foundational mathematical source named in formula_authorization. Reviews are used for coverage and consistency, not to invent formulas.
interpretation.association_rule: An association with later citations supports a publication-time predictor role only. It does not establish causality, quality, correctness, or innovation.
interpretation.negative_evidence_rule: Mixed, null, adverse, and construct-validity findings are retained and can restrict a feature to sensitivity analysis or exclude it.

records.citation: Uzzi B, Mukherjee S, Stringer M, Jones B (2013). Atypical combinations and scientific impact. Science 342:468-472.
records.finding: High-impact work was associated with a conventional core combined with an atypical tail rather than uniformly unusual combinations.
records.limitations: Journal-pair units and a contemporaneous null model do not automatically establish direct paper novelty; temporal implementation must be made strictly prior.

records.citation: Kim D, Cerigo DB, Jeong H, Youn H (2016). Technological novelty profile and invention's future impact. EPJ Data Science 5:8.
records.finding: Patent inventions with a conventional core and a novel addition had higher subsequent citation impact than uniformly conventional or uniformly unusual profiles.
records.limitations: Technology-code patent setting; transfer to scientific cited-source pairs depends on the independent paper applications and local T0 audit.

records.citation: Lee YN, Walsh JP, Wang J (2015). Creativity in scientific teams: Unpacking novelty and impact. Research Policy 44:684-697.
records.finding: Team size had an inverted-U association with novelty but a rising association with high impact, showing that novelty and impact should be modeled separately.
records.limitations: Observational design; cited-journal combinations capture only recombinational novelty.

records.citation: Wang J, Veugelers R, Stephan P (2017). Bias against novelty in science: A cautionary tale for users of bibliometric indicators. Research Policy 46:1416-1436.
records.finding: First-time knowledge combinations were linked to delayed recognition, motivating publication-time novelty features and fixed-horizon outcome separation.
records.limitations: First occurrence is sensitive to database coverage and knowledge-unit choice.

records.citation: Bornmann L, Tekles A, Zhang HH, Ye FY (2019). Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references? A validation study of bibliometric novelty indicators based on F1000Prime data. Journal of Informetrics 13:100979.
records.finding: Only one of the evaluated unusual-combination indicators showed convergent validity with expert novelty assessments.
records.limitations: Biomedical expert recommendations and validation labels may not generalize to all fields.

records.citation: Fontana M, Iori M, Montobbio F, Sinatra R (2020). New and atypical combinations: An assessment of novelty and interdisciplinarity. Research Policy 49:104063.
records.finding: First-combination novelty had weak discrimination in the tested physics corpus, while atypical-combination novelty overlapped with interdisciplinarity.
records.limitations: APS physics corpus; results nevertheless require separate construct labels and supporting rather than sole-indicator use.

records.citation: Yin D, Wu Z, Yokota K, Matsumoto K, Shibayama S (2023). Identify novel elements of knowledge with word embedding. PLOS ONE 18:e0284567.
records.study_type: primary method and author-survey validation study
records.finding: Text-based element novelty correlated with author-reported discovery novelty across fields.
records.limitations: Requires complete title/abstract text and a frozen historically bounded embedding model, neither available in the audited local data.

records.citation: Matsumoto K, Shibayama S, Kang B, Igami M (2021). Introducing a novelty indicator for scientific research: validating the knowledge-based combinatorial approach. Scientometrics 126:6891-6915.
records.study_type: primary method and researcher-survey validation study
formula_authorization: mean Jaccard dissimilarity between a focal reference set and pre-existing same-domain paper reference sets
records.finding: Reference-set dissimilarity was positively associated with researchers' subjective novelty assessments across natural-science fields.
records.limitations: Validation used 1,871 Japanese papers and survey judgments; comparison-universe and field-taxonomy adaptations must be frozen.

records.citation: Stirling A (2007). A general framework for analysing diversity in science, technology and society. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 4:707-719.
records.finding: Diversity must be decomposed into variety, balance, and disparity rather than represented by an undefined single score.
records.limitations: A general framework, not an article-level future-impact validation.

records.citation: Rafols I, Meyer M (2010). Diversity and network coherence as indicators of interdisciplinarity: case studies in bionanoscience. Scientometrics 82:263-287.
records.finding: Diversity and coherence provide distinct views of interdisciplinarity.
records.limitations: Case-study setting; no universal monotonic impact claim.

records.citation: Wang J, Thijs B, Glanzel W (2015). Interdisciplinarity and Impact: Distinct Effects of Variety, Balance, and Disparity. PLOS ONE 10:e0127298.
records.finding: Variety, balance, and disparity had distinct, partly nonlinear associations with citation impact.
records.limitations: Associations vary by component and field; no single diversity score should be assumed monotonic.

records.citation: Yegros-Yegros A, Rafols I, D'Este P (2015). Does interdisciplinary research lead to higher citation impact? The different effect of proximal and distal interdisciplinarity. PLOS ONE 10:e0135095.
records.finding: Proximal and distal interdisciplinarity related differently to impact, and some associations were inverted-U shaped.
records.limitations: Results depend on field classification and distance definition.

records.citation: Leydesdorff L, Wagner CS, Bornmann L (2019). Interdisciplinarity as diversity in citation patterns among journals: Rao-Stirling diversity, relative variety, and the Gini coefficient. Journal of Informetrics 13:255-269.
records.finding: Alternative diversity indicators capture different components and can rank units differently.
records.limitations: Journal-level comparisons; supports component separation rather than a unique article-level composite.

records.citation: Mukherjee S, Romero DM, Jones B, Uzzi B (2017). The nearly universal link between the age of past knowledge and tomorrow's breakthroughs in science and technology. Science Advances 3:e1601315.
formula_authorization: coefficient of variation of reference age
records.finding: Breakthrough probability was elevated for work combining a relatively recent knowledge center with broad reference-age variation across science and technology.
records.limitations: The source's binary hotspot regions are descriptive; this protocol retains continuous mean and coefficient of variation.

records.citation: Didegah F, Thelwall M (2013). Which factors help authors produce the highest impact research? Collaboration, journal and document properties. Journal of Informetrics 7:861-873.
records.finding: Reference count and cited-reference impact were associated with citations; collaboration effects varied; title length and readability were null or practically small.
records.limitations: Observational and field-dependent; journal impact factor is not admitted by this protocol.

records.citation: Didegah F, Thelwall M (2013). Determinants of research citation impact in nanoscience and nanotechnology. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology 64:1055-1064.
records.finding: Publication-time journal and cited-reference impact were strong determinants in nanoscience; several authorship metrics were inconsistent.
records.limitations: Single domain and observational; journal prestige scores are excluded here.

records.citation: Yan E (2014). Research dynamics: Measuring the continuity and popularity of research topics. Journal of Informetrics 8:98-110.
records.finding: Topic continuity and popularity can be measured from longitudinal publication histories.
records.limitations: Topic definitions are taxonomy-dependent and do not measure focal-paper quality.

records.citation: Klavans R, Boyack KW (2017). Research portfolio analysis and topic prominence. Journal of Informetrics 11:1158-1174.
records.finding: Topic prominence captures visibility, momentum, and demand at the research-option level.
records.limitations: The full prominence composite includes variables not locally audited; only prior volume and growth inputs are retained.

records.citation: Hu YH, Tai CT, Liu KE, Cai CF (2020). Identification of highly-cited papers using topic-model-based and bibliometric features: The consideration of keyword popularity. Journal of Informetrics 14:101004.
records.finding: Keyword-popularity features improved highly cited-paper prediction in the studied discipline.
records.limitations: Results were discipline-specific and keyword/topic mappings may be retrospective.

records.citation: Wuchty S, Jones BF, Uzzi B (2007). The increasing dominance of teams in production of knowledge. Science 316:1036-1039.
records.finding: Team-produced work became more prevalent and was frequently more highly cited than solo work.
records.limitations: Team size mixes capacity and visibility and is not a direct measure of innovation.

records.citation: Lariviere V, Gingras Y, Sugimoto CR, Tsou A (2015). Team size matters: Collaboration and scientific impact since 1900. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology 66:1323-1332.
records.finding: Collaboration scale and impact associations changed across fields and historical periods.
records.limitations: Requires field-year context and should not be interpreted causally.

records.citation: Wu L, Wang D, Evans JA (2019). Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology. Nature 566:378-382.
records.finding: Large teams tended to develop existing lines while small teams were more disruptive, so team size is an opportunity/context feature rather than innovation evidence.
records.limitations: Disruption is a future outcome and cannot enter the T0 feature set.

records.citation: Sinatra R, Wang D, Deville P, Song C, Barabasi AL (2016). Quantifying the evolution of individual scientific impact. Science 354:aaf5239.
records.finding: Career impact combines persistent individual parameters and stochastic timing, cautioning against treating prior productivity as scientific merit.
records.limitations: Author-level model; the local prior-output feature covers only the Nature cohort.

records.citation: Petersen AM, Fortunato S, Pan RK, Kaski K, Penner O, Rungi A, Riccaboni M, Stanley HE, Pammolli F (2014). Reputation and impact in academic careers. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111:15316-15321.
records.finding: Prior reputation and cumulative advantage shape later citation opportunity.
records.limitations: Reputation is a structural opportunity mechanism; prestige scores are excluded by the fairness rule.

records.citation: Biscaro C, Giupponi C (2014). Co-Authorship and Bibliographic Coupling Network Effects on Citations. PLOS ONE 9:e99502.
records.finding: Coauthorship and bibliographic-coupling positions showed heterogeneous citation associations.
records.limitations: Single empirical setting and mixed signs; network variables are opportunity features.

records.citation: Guan J, Yan Y, Zhang JJ (2017). The impact of collaboration and knowledge networks on citations. Journal of Informetrics 11:407-422.
records.finding: Collaboration and knowledge-network positions were associated with citation outcomes.
records.limitations: Observational; exact network construction affects estimates.

records.citation: Sarigol E, Pfitzner R, Scholtes I, Garas A, Schweitzer F (2014). Predicting scientific success based on coauthorship networks. EPJ Data Science 3:9.
records.finding: Pre-publication coauthorship centralities predicted highly cited papers in computer science and were explicitly interpreted as social visibility.
records.limitations: Computer-science sample and author-network inputs are not materialized locally.

records.citation: Letchford A, Moat HS, Preis T (2015). The advantage of short paper titles. Royal Society Open Science 2:150266.
records.finding: Shorter titles were associated with more citations in the sampled highly cited literature.
records.limitations: Selection and journal-level confounding make title length a sensitivity-only feature.

records.citation: Letchford A, Preis T, Moat HS (2016). The advantage of simple paper abstracts. Journal of Informetrics 10:1-8.
records.finding: Simpler abstracts were associated with citation attention.
records.limitations: Observational and text unavailable locally; related studies report null or very small readability effects.

records.citation: Davis PM, Lewenstein BV, Simon DH, Booth JG, Connolly MJL (2008). Open access publishing, article downloads, and citations: randomised controlled trial. BMJ 337:a568.
records.finding: Open access increased downloads but did not produce an early citation advantage in the randomized comparison.
records.limitations: Short citation horizon and selected journals; historical T0 OA status is unavailable locally.

records.citation: Davis PM (2011). Open access, readership, citations: a randomized controlled trial of scientific journal publishing. FASEB Journal 25:2129-2134.
records.finding: Randomized open access increased readership without a clear citation advantage.
records.limitations: Publisher trial; local historical status is not audited.

records.citation: Piwowar HA, Day RS, Fridsma DB (2007). Sharing detailed research data is associated with increased citation rate. PLOS ONE 2:e308.
records.finding: Detailed data sharing was associated with higher citations.
records.limitations: Observational, biomedical, and vulnerable to selection; historical repository linkage is unavailable locally.

records.citation: Piwowar HA, Vision TJ (2013). Data reuse and the open data citation advantage. PeerJ 1:e175.
records.finding: Archived data were associated with citation advantage and measurable reuse.
records.limitations: Observational and domain-specific; publication-time status cannot be reconstructed for the full local corpus.

records.citation: Colavizza G, Hrynaszkiewicz I, Staden I, Whitaker K, McGillivray B (2020). The citation advantage of linking publications to research data. PLOS ONE 15:e0230416.
records.finding: Formal links to research data were associated with citation advantage.
records.limitations: Observational; status and link timing are not historically audited locally.

records.citation: Fraser N, Momeni F, Mayr P, Peters I (2020). The relationship between bioRxiv preprints, citations and altmetrics. Quantitative Science Studies 1:618-638.
records.finding: Articles deposited in bioRxiv before journal publication had higher citation and online-attention counts than matched nondeposited articles.
records.limitations: Observational biological-science study with unresolved selection effects; complete preprint linkage is unavailable locally.

records.citation: Tahamtan I, Safipour Afshar A, Ahamdzadeh K (2016). Factors affecting number of citations: a comprehensive review of the literature. Scientometrics 107:1195-1225.
records.finding: Citation determinants span paper, journal, author, field, and access properties, with substantial heterogeneity.
records.limitations: Review evidence does not authorize new formulas and many reported determinants are confounded.

records.citation: Tahamtan I, Bornmann L (2019). What do citation counts measure? An updated review of studies on citations in scientific documents published between 2006 and 2018. Scientometrics 121:1635-1684.
records.finding: Citations reflect multiple scientific and non-scientific processes and cannot be equated with quality.
records.limitations: Narrative synthesis with heterogeneous designs.

records.citation: Mammola S, Piano E, Doretto A, Caprio E, Chamberlain D (2022). Measuring the influence of non-scientific features on citations. Scientometrics 127:4123-4137.
records.finding: Across 262 meta-analyzed studies, non-scientific feature effects were consistently weak in magnitude.
records.limitations: Heterogeneous feature definitions and observational evidence; supports separate opportunity blocks.

records.citation: Bornmann L, Daniel HD (2008). What do citation counts measure? A review of studies on citing behavior. Journal of Documentation 64:45-80.
records.finding: Citation behavior is multidimensional and varies by field and opportunity.
records.limitations: Does not imply that field controls remove all citation bias.

records.citation: Aksnes DW, Langfeldt L, Wouters P (2019). Citations, Citation Indicators, and Research Quality: An Overview of Basic Concepts and Theories. SAGE Open 9:2158244019829575.
records.finding: Citations may reflect scientific relevance and impact but do not establish soundness, originality, or societal value.
records.limitations: Conceptual synthesis rather than a feature-validation study.

records.citation: Nieminen P, Carpenter J, Rucker G, Schumacher M (2006). The relationship between quality of research and citation frequency. BMC Medical Research Methodology 6:42.
records.finding: Methodological and statistical quality were not consistently related to citation frequency.
records.limitations: Biomedical focus; reinforces construct separation rather than proving no relation in every field.

records.citation: Duyx B, Urlings MJE, Swaen GMH, Bouter LM, Zeegers MP (2017). Scientific citations favor positive results: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 88:92-101.
records.finding: Statistically significant and hypothesis-supporting findings received more citations, demonstrating outcome-dependent citation bias.
records.limitations: Bias strength varies by discipline; positive-result status is explicitly forbidden as a training feature.

records.citation: Jannot AS, Agoritsas T, Gayet-Ageron A, Perneger TV (2013). Citation bias favoring statistically significant studies was present in medical research. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 66:296-301.
records.finding: Statistically significant medical studies were preferentially cited.
records.limitations: Medical setting, but sufficient to prohibit a positive-result predictor in a general model.
